name: MDX

name: MDX landscape assessment
judgementReason: Multidimensional query language; surviving only in MS Analysis Services.

name: Substrait
statusStatement: Stable; growing adoption across query engines
whyAStandard: Substrait is published as an open specification with protobuf-defined plan types, governed by an independent, ASF-inspired PMC. Multiple independent engines consume and produce Substrait plans, which is exactly the cross-vendor interchange contract that makes it a standard rather than a project.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Substrait landscape assessment
judgementReason: Cross-engine query-plan IR — pick when you're building or integrating engines that need a portable plan format; end users rarely touch it.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: OpenTelemetry
governanceStatement: CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation), Linux Foundation
statusStatement: Stable; widely adopted across cloud-native stacks
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: OpenTelemetry landscape assessment
judgementReason: Vendor-neutral observability standard.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: OORS
statusStatement: Emerging — auxiliary BITOL standard, not yet released
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: OORS landscape assessment
judgementReason: BITOL observability/quality-result standard; new and under-adopted.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: ODCS landscape assessment
judgementReason: Winning data-contract spec; YAML, multi-vendor.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: OpenAPI landscape assessment
judgementReason: De-facto REST description with tooling for almost every language.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: AsyncAPI landscape assessment
judgementReason: The OpenAPI-equivalent for event APIs once you commit to documenting them.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: GraphQL landscape assessment
judgementReason: Default for client-driven aggregation; mature spec, multi-language tooling, well-established at scale.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: gRPC landscape assessment
judgementReason: Right for service-to-service binary RPC; wrong for browser clients.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: dbt
statusStatement: De-facto standard for analytics engineering; vendor-governed format
whyAStandard: The dbt project artefacts — the manifest.json, the model YAML, the schema.yml tests — have become the interchange format for analytics engineering. SQLMesh, Lightdash, Elementary, dbt-osmosis and many other tools read or emit dbt's project structure rather than inventing their own. Quality checks declared in dbt are part of that surface. That makes the format itself the standard, even though dbt Labs governs it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: dbt landscape assessment
judgementReason: Analytics-engineering default: SQL-first models, tests, lineage.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Great Expectations
whyAStandard: The expectations DSL and the JSON validation-result schema GX defines have become the reference vocabulary for declarative data quality in Python. Other tools embed or interoperate with Great Expectations rather than reinvent the same primitives. The standard part is the expectation language and its result format — not the company behind it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Great Expectations landscape assessment
judgementReason: Python-first DQ; powerful but heavy.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: dbt tests
statusStatement: De-facto for analytics teams already on dbt
whyAStandard: dbt's test definitions and the manifest entries they produce are what other DQ tools (Elementary, re_data, dbt-osmosis) read. The format is the standard surface even though dbt Labs governs it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: dbt tests landscape assessment
judgementReason: Right when your transformations already live in dbt; otherwise reach for a standalone DQ tool.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: SodaCL
whyAStandard: SodaCL is the YAML check language Soda publishes — and the part that other tools have standardised on. The Data Contract CLI delegates ODCS quality checks to SodaCL because expressing checks portably matters more than running them in Soda Cloud. The check syntax is the standard surface, even though Soda governs it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: SodaCL landscape assessment
judgementReason: YAML-first DQ; lighter than Great Expectations, smaller ecosystem.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: ODPS landscape assessment
judgementReason: Winning data-product spec; ODCS-aligned.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: DPDS landscape assessment
judgementReason: Coexists with BITOL's ODPS but with smaller community.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: ODPS landscape assessment
judgementReason: LF-governed data-product spec; strong on commercial terms, modest adoption.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: DPROD
governanceStatement: EKGF / Object Management Group (OMG) — RDF/OWL vocabulary
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: DPROD landscape assessment
judgementReason: RDF/OWL data-product vocabulary; right only when your stack already lives in linked data.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Iceberg
statusStatement: Stable; effectively the winner of the table-format race
whyAStandard: Iceberg's table-format specification — manifest files, metadata layout, snapshot semantics — is published openly and re-implemented by every major engine: Snowflake, Databricks, Trino, Spark, Dremio, DuckDB. The format itself is the standard; the original Netflix implementation is just one client of it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Iceberg landscape assessment
judgementReason: Default open table format for new lakes; multi-vendor catalog support and ASF governance.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Delta
whyAStandard: The Delta transaction-log protocol is published as an open spec and implemented by readers and writers beyond Databricks — delta-rs, Trino, Flink, Spark. The standard surface is the protocol, not the Databricks runtime; that is what makes a Delta table portable across engines.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Delta landscape assessment
judgementReason: Reach-For if you're on Databricks; Situational elsewhere.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Hudi
whyAStandard: Hudi publishes its on-disk table format and timeline protocol as an open spec, and engines beyond the Hudi runtime (Spark, Flink, Trino, Presto) read and write it directly. The format is the standard part; the platform tooling is one implementation of it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Hudi landscape assessment
judgementReason: Third-place table format; legitimate CDC-upsert use cases but lost the default slot.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: DuckLake
statusStatement: Emerging; v1.0 production-ready (April 2026), adoption concentrated in the DuckDB ecosystem
whyAStandard: DuckLake's catalog schema is published as an open SQL specification — any database that speaks SQL can host a DuckLake catalog. Listed on the de-facto criterion: the schema is the standard surface, even though DuckDB Labs governs it and adoption is still early.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: DuckLake landscape assessment
judgementReason: DuckDB-Labs catalog; v1.0 production-ready, ecosystem still small.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: XML Schema landscape assessment
judgementReason: The schema language for XML — load-bearing in enterprise integration, finance, healthcare, and government with mature tooling.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: JSON Schema
statusStatement: Latest draft 2020-12; published independently after leaving the IETF Internet-Draft track
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: JSON Schema landscape assessment
judgementReason: Default API-payload validation; behind OpenAPI/AsyncAPI.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: SQL DDL landscape assessment
judgementReason: Universal way to describe a relational schema; portable across engines.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: AVRO Schema landscape assessment
judgementReason: Schema language for Kafka payloads; pairs with Schema Registry.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Protobuf
statusStatement: Stable; de-facto schema for binary RPC
whyAStandard: The .proto language and the wire format are publicly specified, with compilers and runtimes for every major language. gRPC, Schema Registry, and countless internal RPC stacks depend on the format definition rather than Google's implementation. That is the standard surface, even though Google governs it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Protobuf landscape assessment
judgementReason: Strong schema-evolution rules; default for gRPC.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Iceberg Catalog
statusStatement: Stable; rapidly becoming the default catalog protocol
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Iceberg Catalog landscape assessment
judgementReason: Canonical catalog API for Iceberg; multi-vendor implementations.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Unity Catalog
whyAStandard: Unity Catalog publishes a public REST API that other catalogs and engines can implement and consume. The API is the standard surface — that is what makes "speaks Unity" a portability claim rather than a Databricks lock-in. The reference implementation is open source under the Linux Foundation.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Unity Catalog landscape assessment
judgementReason: LF-open-sourced but still Databricks-tilted in practice.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Hive Metastore
statusStatement: Stable; ubiquitous in lakehouse engines, slowly being replaced by Iceberg REST and Unity Catalog
whyAStandard: The Hive Metastore Thrift API is publicly defined and re-implemented by every major lakehouse engine. "Speaks the Hive Metastore API" became the portability test for a generation of big-data tools — the API is the standard, independent of the original Hive server.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Hive Metastore landscape assessment
judgementReason: The catalog Iceberg REST is displacing; maintain only.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Schema Registry
whyAStandard: Confluent's Schema Registry REST API is publicly documented and re-implemented by Apicurio (Red Hat), AWS Glue, Karapace (Aiven), and Redpanda. Producers and consumers depend on the API contract, not on Confluent's server — which is what promotes it from a vendor product to a de-facto standard.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Schema Registry landscape assessment
judgementReason: The default Kafka schema-management surface.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: CSV
statusStatement: Stable; the lowest common denominator for tabular data
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: CSV landscape assessment
judgementReason: Universal flat file; ugly but ubiquitous.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: JSON landscape assessment
judgementReason: Universal payload format; not a choice.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: XML
statusStatement: Stable since 1998; XML 1.0 (Fifth Edition, 2008) is the de-facto current spec
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: XML landscape assessment
judgementReason: Load-bearing in finance, healthcare, and government; mature tooling around XSD, XSLT, XPath, XQuery.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: YAML landscape assessment
judgementReason: Default surface for config and contract specs.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: PARQUET
whyAStandard: Parquet's on-disk format is published as an open spec with independent reader/writer implementations in C++, Java, Rust, Go, and Python. Every analytics engine and lakehouse format depends on the format spec, not on a particular library. That makes the file format itself the standard.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: PARQUET landscape assessment
judgementReason: De-facto columnar storage; baseline for analytics.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: AVRO
whyAStandard: The Avro container format and binary encoding are open specifications with independent implementations across Java, Python, Go, C++, and Rust. Kafka, Schema Registry, and most stream processors depend on the format spec, not on a particular Avro library — which is what makes it portable.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: AVRO landscape assessment
judgementReason: Kafka's binary payload of choice; first-class with Schema Registry.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: ORC
statusStatement: Stable; mostly seen in Hive-era stacks
whyAStandard: ORC's on-disk format is an open Apache spec with independent readers in Java, C++, and Rust. Hive, Spark, Trino, Presto and others read and write the same files because they target the format, not a single library. The file format is the standard surface.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: ORC landscape assessment
judgementReason: Pick if you're in Hive/Tez territory; otherwise Parquet wins.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Lance
governanceStatement: Lance community (independent open source, LF-inspired governance)
statusStatement: Emerging; production use concentrated in AI/ML stacks
whyAStandard: Lance's on-disk format is published as an open spec with independent Rust and Python implementations. LanceDB, DataFusion, DuckDB integrations, and downstream tools target the format itself rather than a single library — putting it on the de-facto standard track under an open, LF-style community governance model.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Lance landscape assessment
judgementReason: AI/ML-optimised columnar format; trajectory good, adoption concentrated.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: OpenLineage landscape assessment
judgementReason: The lineage-emission standard, with column-level support.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: OPA
statusStatement: Stable; de-facto policy engine for cloud-native
whyAStandard: Rego — the policy language OPA defines — has become the portable way to express authorization rules across cloud-native systems. Kubernetes admission control, service meshes, CI gates, and data-mesh governance all consume the same Rego policies. The language and the OPA evaluation API are the standard, with multiple compatible runtimes.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: OPA landscape assessment
judgementReason: General-purpose policy engine; mature Rego ecosystem.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: MCP landscape assessment

name: A2A

name: A2A landscape assessment

:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: S3
whyAStandard: AWS publishes the S3 REST API, and MinIO, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Ceph RGW, GCS interop, and most on-prem object stores re-implement it. "Speaks S3" is treated as a portability guarantee precisely because the API surface — not AWS's server — is what tools depend on.

name: S3 landscape assessment

statusStatement: Stable; foundation of the semantic web

name: RDF/OWL landscape assessment

name: SKOS landscape assessment

name: JSON-LD landscape assessment
judgementReason: Pragmatic semantic-web on-ramp inside ordinary JSON.

:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: SPARQL landscape assessment
judgementReason: Query RDF; right when your data lives in triples.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: HDFS
statusStatement: Stable; mature, declining in greenfield projects
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: HDFS landscape assessment
judgementReason: Hadoop-era distributed FS; object storage replaced it for nearly all new builds.

name: JDBC landscape assessment
judgementReason: Every JVM data tool speaks it; default for 25 years.

name: ODBC landscape assessment

governanceStatement: XMLA Council (Microsoft, Hyperion, SAS); de-facto industry spec
statusStatement: Legacy; still the standard wire protocol for OLAP/semantic-layer access

name: XMLA landscape assessment
judgementReason: Legacy SOAP-based BI protocol; survives only inside MS Analysis Services.

name: ADBC
whyAStandard: ADBC is published as an open API specification under the Apache Arrow project, with drivers contributed by multiple vendors (Snowflake, BigQuery, DuckDB, Postgres, SQLite). The driver interface and the Arrow-batch result contract are the standard surface — like JDBC/ODBC, but columnar.

name: ADBC landscape assessment
judgementReason: Arrow-native DB connectivity; the modern replacement for JDBC/ODBC on analytical workloads.

name: Quack
statusStatement: Emerging; new client-server protocol from the DuckDB ecosystem
whyAStandard: Quack is published as an open protocol specification by DuckDB Labs. Listed on the de-facto criterion: the wire format is the standard surface, even though governance sits with a single vendor and adoption is still concentrated in the DuckDB ecosystem.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Quack landscape assessment
judgementReason: DuckDB's new client-server protocol; promising but early — watch adoption beyond the DuckDB ecosystem.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: HTTP landscape assessment
judgementReason: Universal application transport; nobody decides to use it.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Kafka
whyAStandard: The Kafka wire protocol is publicly documented and re-implemented by Redpanda, WarpStream, and AutoMQ — clients written for one server work against the others. The standard surface is the protocol, not the Apache Kafka broker; that is what lets producers and consumers stay portable across vendors.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Kafka landscape assessment
judgementReason: The streaming backbone; competitors challenge the implementation, not the category.

name: MQTT landscape assessment
judgementReason: Excellent in IoT/edge, irrelevant outside it.

name: CloudEvents landscape assessment
judgementReason: Default event envelope; HTTP/Kafka/AMQP/MQTT bindings all standardised.

name: AMQP landscape assessment
judgementReason: Pick when you want broker semantics (RabbitMQ-shaped problems).
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: JMS landscape assessment
judgementReason: Java-only messaging API; maintain if you have it, don't pick it new.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: FTP / SFTP
fullName: File Transfer Protocol / SSH File Transfer Protocol
statusStatement: Stable; legacy but pervasive in B2B data exchange
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: FTP / SFTP landscape assessment
judgementReason: Unencrypted FTP is unsafe for new work; SFTP-only as a last resort when partners can't speak HTTP APIs.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Delta Sharing
whyAStandard: Delta Sharing is published as an open REST protocol specification under the Linux Foundation, with reference servers and clients across multiple languages and several independent implementations (Databricks, AWS, Azure, Power BI). The wire protocol is the standard surface — not the Databricks product.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Delta Sharing landscape assessment
judgementReason: Cross-org sharing without copies; well-defined niche.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: DataFrame API
governanceStatement: Consortium for Python Data API Standards (data-apis.org)
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: DataFrame API landscape assessment
judgementReason: Portable Python DataFrame spec; the way to write library code that runs on pandas, Polars, Modin, and cuDF.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Apache Arrow
statusStatement: Stable; broadly adopted across the analytics stack
whyAStandard: Arrow's columnar memory layout and IPC format are an open specification, not a library. DuckDB, Polars, pandas 2.x, Spark, and ADBC all align on the same in-memory representation, which is what enables zero-copy interchange across engines and languages. The format spec is the standard.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Apache Arrow landscape assessment
judgementReason: In-memory columnar standard powering Flight, ADBC, DataFusion, Polars.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Spark
whyAStandard: Spark's DataFrame API and the Spark Connect protocol are the standard parts. Spark Connect publishes a gRPC contract that any Spark-compatible engine can serve, and the DataFrame API is what other engines (e.g. Databricks Connect, Apache Sedona) target. The interface, not the JVM runtime, is what makes Spark a standard.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Spark landscape assessment
judgementReason: Default distributed batch+streaming engine.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Beam
whyAStandard: Beam's value is the model, not the runner. The Beam programming model and the portability framework (Fn API, Runner API) are an open specification that multiple runners implement. Pipelines move between Flink, Spark, and Dataflow without code changes precisely because all three implement the same Beam contract — making the model the standard surface tools and teams target.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Beam landscape assessment
judgementReason: Write once, run on Flink/Spark/Dataflow; right when runner portability matters.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Pandas
statusStatement: Stable; the de-facto Python DataFrame API
whyAStandard: The pandas Python API is the de-facto DataFrame interface other libraries deliberately mimic — Modin, cuDF, Dask, and many wrappers expose pandas-compatible surfaces precisely because users already know it. The API shape, not the implementation, is what makes pandas a standard reference.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Pandas landscape assessment
judgementReason: Universal Python DataFrame; you don't choose it, you encounter it.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Ibis
whyAStandard: Ibis defines a backend-neutral DataFrame expression API, with a published backend protocol that 20+ engines implement. The API and the backend contract are the standard surface — Ibis is the rare project where the standardised "interface" is its whole reason to exist.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Ibis landscape assessment
judgementReason: Portable Python DataFrame compiling to many backends; trajectory strong, footprint small.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: SQL DML
whyAStandard: ISO/IEC 9075 specifies a portable DML core — CTEs (SQL:1999), window functions (SQL:2003), and MERGE (SQL:2003) — that every serious analytical engine implements. Transformations written against this core run on Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, DuckDB, Postgres, and Trino with minimal change. The standard surface, not any vendor's dialect, is what makes SQL the default processing language.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: SQL DML landscape assessment
judgementReason: Portable transformation language across relational/lakehouse engines.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: XSLT
statusStatement: Legacy; XSLT 3.0 (2017) is current, but new adoption is rare
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: XSLT landscape assessment
judgementReason: XML transformation; maintain if you have it, don't pick it new.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: LinkML
statusStatement: Stable; widely used in biomedical and life-sciences data modelling
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: LinkML landscape assessment
judgementReason: Multi-output schema language; strong in biomedical, niche elsewhere.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: schema.org
statusStatement: Stable; mainstream for web structured data, niche in data-architecture contexts
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: schema.org landscape assessment
judgementReason: Web SEO/structured-data vocabulary; different audience from data-platform work.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: ShEx landscape assessment
judgementReason: RDF shape validation parallel to SHACL; smaller community.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: ODRL landscape assessment
judgementReason: Rights-expression language; relevant where data licensing matters.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: PROV landscape assessment
judgementReason: W3C provenance vocabulary; predates OpenLineage by a decade, fading.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: GQL landscape assessment
judgementReason: Vendor-neutral property-graph query language — pick when your stack is already on graph databases.

name: OData
whyAStandard: OData is an OASIS Standard with a publicly-defined wire protocol and metadata format (CSDL). Multiple independent implementations exist across Microsoft, SAP, Salesforce, Oracle, and the OData4j / Olingo open-source stacks, so "speaks OData" is a portability claim rather than a vendor-lock-in label.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: OData landscape assessment
judgementReason: Pick when you live in the Microsoft BI/Dynamics world.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Table Schema landscape assessment
judgementReason: Lightweight Frictionless tabular spec; small ecosystem.
:LABEL: LandscapeAssessment

name: Apache Airflow
statusStatement: Stable; mature platform for scheduled, finite batch workflows
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Apache Airflow landscape assessment
judgementReason: Mature and widely supported for scheduled, finite batch workflows; consider alternatives for highly dynamic, decentralised or continuously running event-stream workloads.

name: Prefect
statusStatement: Actively maintained open-source workflow orchestration platform
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataStandardLandscapeEntry

name: Prefect landscape assessment
judgementReason: Python-native orchestration with dynamic workflows, retries, state tracking and transactional controls; promising for data pipelines, but independent evidence remains limited and governance is vendor-led.

name: Temporal landscape assessment
judgementReason: Strong choice when durable execution, recovery and long-running workflow state are primary requirements; less data-pipeline-specific than conventional orchestrators and requires additional operational commitment.

name: GDPR
description: The EU's personal data regime: lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, data subject rights, records of processing, transfer rules, and breach notification within 72 hours. | For a data platform it is the source of most catalogue metadata obligations you cannot avoid: what personal data you hold, why you hold it, who it goes to, and how long you keep it. ISO/IEC 27701 and the EU Cloud Code of Conduct are the usual ways of evidencing it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: EU AI Act
statusStatement: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; prohibitions since February 2025, general-purpose AI rules since August 2025, high-risk obligations from 2027
description: A risk-tiered regime for AI systems: prohibited practices, obligations for high-risk systems (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy and robustness), transparency duties, and a separate track for general-purpose AI models. | Its data governance article is the one that lands on data teams: training, validation and test data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and as far as possible free of errors and complete. ISO/IEC 42001 and the forthcoming CEN-CENELEC standards are how conformity gets demonstrated.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: Data Act
statusStatement: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854; in force January 2024, applicable since 12 September 2025
description: Rules on access to and use of data generated by connected products and related services: users get access to the data their devices produce and can direct it to third parties, with contractual fairness rules and safeguards against unlawful international access. | It also mandates cloud switching and interoperability, removing egress charges over time and requiring providers to support portability. That makes open formats and portable contracts a legal argument, not only an architectural preference.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: DGA
description: The framework for data sharing across the EU: re-use of protected public sector data, a notification regime for data intermediation services, and rules for recognised data altruism organisations. | It is the legal scaffolding under the European data spaces, and the reason the Dataspace Protocol, Gaia-X and the DSSC Blueprint exist as concrete implementations rather than position papers.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: NIS2
statusStatement: Directive (EU) 2022/2555; national transposition was due October 2024, and several member states ran late
description: Cybersecurity risk management and incident reporting duties for essential and important entities across energy, transport, health, digital infrastructure, public administration and more, with management bodies personally accountable for compliance. | Being a directive, what binds you is the national transposition, not the text itself, so the detail varies by member state. ISO/IEC 27001 and IT-Grundschutz are the usual routes to demonstrating the required measures.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: DORA
description: ICT risk management, incident classification and reporting, resilience testing, and third-party risk oversight for financial entities, plus a supervisory regime for critical ICT providers serving them. | The third-party chapter is what reaches data platforms: a register of information on every ICT contract, mandated contractual terms, exit strategies, and concentration risk analysis. Your data vendors become items in a supervisory filing.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: CRA
statusStatement: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847; reporting from September 2026, main obligations from December 2027
description: Cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements placed on the EU market: secure-by-design obligations, vulnerability handling for the support period, and reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities. | It puts an SBOM obligation into EU law for the first time, which is why SPDX and CycloneDX moved from good practice to procurement requirement.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: BCBS 239
fullName: Principles for Effective Risk Data Aggregation and Risk Reporting
description: Fourteen principles on governance, data architecture, accuracy, completeness, timeliness and adaptability of risk data, written for global systemically important banks after the financial crisis exposed how few could aggregate their own exposures quickly. | It is the closest thing to a regulation about data architecture itself, and the reason lineage, ownership and data quality metrics are audited artefacts in banking. DCAM is the usual assessment vehicle.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: SOX
statusStatement: Enacted 2002; Sections 302 and 404 drive the controls work
description: Requires management and auditors to assess and attest to internal control over financial reporting, with personal certification by the CEO and CFO. | Section 404 is why access controls, change management and audit trails on financial data pipelines are tested annually. Any data product feeding the numbers in a listed company's filings is in scope.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: HIPAA
fullName: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
statusStatement: Enacted 1996; Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules
description: The US regime for protected health information: the Privacy Rule on permitted use and disclosure, the Security Rule on administrative, physical and technical safeguards, and mandatory breach notification. | Its business associate agreements pull every downstream processor into scope, which is why de-identification and minimum-necessary access are design constraints on any health data platform touching the US.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: CCPA / CPRA
fullName: California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended
statusStatement: CCPA 2018, amended by CPRA; enforced by the CPPA
description: California's consumer privacy regime: rights to know, delete, correct and opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information, plus limits on the use of sensitive personal information. | It is the template most other US state privacy laws copied, so building for CCPA generally buys you the rest of the patchwork: an opt-out signal and a deletion path that actually reaches every downstream copy.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: DAMA-DMBOK2
fullName: Data Management Body of Knowledge, 2nd Edition
statusStatement: 2nd edition (2017), revised 2024; a DMBOK 3.0 project started in 2025
description: The reference body of knowledge for enterprise data management, organised around eleven knowledge areas: governance, architecture, modelling, storage, security, integration, reference and master data, warehousing, metadata, quality, and document management. | It is not a certifiable standard and prescribes no controls. Its value under regulatory pressure is the shared vocabulary: when an auditor asks who owns a data set and how its quality is measured, DMBOK gives you the roles and processes to point at.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: DCAM
statusStatement: v3: eight components, 34 capabilities and 101 sub-capabilities
description: A capability assessment model that scores an organisation's data management maturity across eight components, from data governance and architecture to data quality and technology architecture, broken down into 34 capabilities and 101 sub-capabilities. | Widely used in banking and insurance as the structured evidence base behind BCBS 239 and comparable supervisory expectations. The assessment output is what turns "we manage our data well" into a defensible score with a remediation roadmap, run in-house or through an authorised partner.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: CDMC
description: A framework for managing and protecting sensitive data in cloud, multi-cloud and hybrid environments, built around fourteen key controls covering classification, ownership, cataloguing, entitlements, and data sovereignty. | It is the cloud-native complement to DCAM rather than a replacement: the key controls are written to be automatable, which makes CDMC the more practical fit when your evidence has to come out of a lakehouse rather than a policy document.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 38505
description: Applies the ISO/IEC 38500 IT governance principles specifically to data, giving boards and executives a model for the accountability, strategy and conformance of data use. | Deliberately high level: it tells a governing body what questions to ask, not how to implement controls. Pair it with a control framework if you need something auditable.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO 8000
statusStatement: Multi-part series; parts published from 2009 onwards
description: A multi-part standard for data quality, best known for its master data parts: syntax, semantic encoding, provenance and the requirements a data set must meet to be exchanged between organisations without loss of meaning. | It is the standard cited when quality has to be a contractual property of the data itself rather than a property of the pipeline that produced it, which is exactly the framing supply chain and product data regulation tends to use.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 11179
description: Specifies how data elements are named, defined, classified and registered so that meaning survives movement between systems and organisations. It is the metadata registry model underneath national statistics offices, health data authorities and public sector registries. | Heavyweight for a product team, but if you file data to a regulator that runs an 11179 registry, its concepts (data element concept, value domain, conceptual domain) are the shape your submissions have to take.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 25012
statusStatement: Published 2008; part of the SQuaRE series
description: Defines a general data quality model with fifteen characteristics (accuracy, completeness, consistency, credibility, currentness, accessibility, compliance, confidentiality, and others), split into inherent and system-dependent views. | Useful as the dictionary behind your data quality checks: when a contract or regulation says data must be "accurate and complete", 25012 is where those words have an agreed definition.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ODRL
description: A policy expression language for permissions, prohibitions and obligations over any asset: who may use this data, for what purpose, under which constraint, and with what duty attached. | It is the vocabulary European data space initiatives use to make terms of use machine-enforceable rather than PDF-shaped. If you need to carry a purpose limitation alongside the data itself, this is the standard to reach for.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: DPV
governanceStatement: W3C Data Privacy Vocabularies and Controls CG
statusStatement: DPV 2.3 (2026); DPVCG report with GDPR, DGA, EHDS and AI Act extensions
description: A vocabulary for expressing personal data handling in machine-readable form: personal data categories, purposes, legal bases, processing operations, recipients, and the technical and organisational measures applied. | Ships with jurisdiction extensions (EU GDPR, EU AI Act, and others), which makes it the practical bridge between a records-of-processing obligation and metadata your catalogue can actually hold.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: OPA
statusStatement: CNCF graduated project since 2021; Rego policy language
description: A general-purpose policy engine with its own declarative language, Rego. Policies are decoupled from the services that enforce them: the service asks OPA for a decision, OPA answers from policy and data. | The compliance value is evidence. Policy is code, decisions are logged, and "access was denied because of clause X" becomes a query rather than an interview.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: XACML
description: The XML policy language and reference architecture that gave attribute-based access control its vocabulary: policy decision point, policy enforcement point, policy information point. | The architecture outlived the syntax. New systems adopt the PDP/PEP split but express the policy in Rego or Cedar; you will still meet XACML in identity and healthcare platforms that standardised on it a decade ago.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 27001
description: The requirements standard for an information security management system: scope, risk assessment, risk treatment, the Annex A control set, and the management processes that keep it alive. | It is the anchor certification of the compliance world. NIS2, DORA and sectoral supervisors do not mandate it by name, but an accredited 27001 certificate is the artefact most readily accepted as evidence that a management system exists.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: NIST CSF
description: An outcome-based framework organised into six functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), each broken into categories and subcategories that describe what good looks like without prescribing how to get there. | Version 2.0 added the Govern function and dropped the critical-infrastructure framing, which is what made it usable as a general risk-communication layer above whatever control catalogue you actually implement.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: NIST RMF
description: The seven-step process (prepare, categorise, select, implement, assess, authorise, monitor) that US federal systems follow to select and authorise security controls from SP 800-53. | It is a process standard, not a control catalogue. Outside the US federal supply chain, the categorise-select-assess loop is worth borrowing even if the authorisation ceremony is not.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: Grundschutz
statusStatement: BSI Standards 200-1, 200-2 and 200-3, with 200-4 for business continuity; Kompendium revised regularly
description: The German federal information security methodology: a modular catalogue of building blocks, each with concrete threats and required safeguards, plus the BSI Standards that describe the management system around them. | Its distinguishing feature is prescriptiveness: where ISO/IEC 27001 says "assess your risk", IT-Grundschutz hands you a baseline of measures per component. Certification is available as ISO/IEC 27001 on the basis of IT-Grundschutz.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 27002
description: The companion control catalogue to ISO/IEC 27001: for each control, what it is for, how to implement it, and what other guidance applies. The 2022 revision restructured 114 controls into 93 across organisational, people, physical and technological themes. | It introduced attributes (control type, security property, operational capability) so controls can be mapped to other frameworks mechanically instead of by hand.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: NIST SP 800-53
fullName: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems
description: A catalogue of over a thousand security and privacy controls across twenty families, with baselines for low, moderate and high impact systems, published free of charge and machine-readable via OSCAL. | Even outside US federal scope it is the reference people map to when two frameworks disagree: 800-53 usually has the finer-grained control that both can point at.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: CIS Controls
statusStatement: v8.1 (June 2024): 18 controls, 153 safeguards, three implementation groups
description: Eighteen prioritised controls with 153 safeguards, split into three implementation groups so a small organisation can implement the first group and honestly claim a baseline. | Paired with the CIS Benchmarks, the hardening configurations for operating systems, cloud services and databases that most CIS-aligned tooling actually checks against.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 27701
statusStatement: 27701:2019 as a 27001 extension; 2025 revision makes it standalone
description: Extends an information security management system into a privacy information management system, with separate requirements for controllers and processors and a mapping annex to GDPR articles. | The GDPR mapping is the reason it matters: it turns "we comply with GDPR" into a set of auditable management-system requirements a certification body can actually test.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 27018
fullName: Protection of PII in Public Clouds
description: A code of practice for public cloud providers acting as processors of personally identifiable information: consent and choice, purpose limitation, disclosure to third parties, return and deletion, and transparency about sub-processors. | Every major cloud provider certifies against it, so it is more often something you inherit from a vendor than something you implement, but it is the right question to ask of any processor in the chain.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: NIST Privacy Framework
description: A voluntary framework structured like the Cybersecurity Framework (Identify, Govern, Control, Communicate, Protect) for managing privacy risk arising from data processing, not only from breaches. | Its useful contribution is separating privacy risk from security risk: problematic data actions can be entirely secure and still harm people. That distinction is what data minimisation and purpose limitation arguments hang on.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 29100
description: The privacy terminology and principles standard: PII, PII principal, PII controller, PII processor, and eleven privacy principles that later ISO privacy standards build on. | Still the normative source of those definitions, but as an implementation target it has been overtaken by ISO/IEC 27701 and the 27018/27550 family.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: MITRE ATT&CK
fullName: Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge
statusStatement: Enterprise, Mobile and ICS matrices; annual releases (v19, April 2026)
description: A curated knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques observed in the wild, organised as matrices and identified by stable technique IDs. | Those IDs are the point. Detections, threat reports, purple-team exercises and supervisory incident reports can all reference the same technique, which is how you answer "are we covered?" with a map rather than an opinion.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: MITRE D3FEND
description: A knowledge graph of defensive techniques across seven tactics (model, harden, detect, isolate, deceive, evict, restore) with explicit digital artefact relationships linking each countermeasure to the offensive techniques it addresses. | Where ATT&CK tells you what attackers do, D3FEND gives you a vocabulary for what your controls actually do about it. Adoption in commercial tooling is growing but not yet the default.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: CWE
statusStatement: Actively maintained; CWE Top 25 published annually
description: A hierarchical catalogue of software and hardware weakness types: the class of flaw (CWE) as distinct from the individual vulnerability instance (CVE). | Static analysis findings, penetration test reports and secure development requirements all reference CWE IDs, which makes it the join key between your scanner output and the control you claim satisfies it.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: CAPEC
fullName: Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification
statusStatement: Actively maintained; cross-referenced with CWE and ATT&CK
description: A catalogue of attack patterns, the method by which a weakness is exploited, cross-referenced to the CWE weaknesses they target and the ATT&CK techniques they realise. | It sits between the two: use it when a threat model needs to explain how a specific weakness becomes a specific technique.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: STIX
statusStatement: STIX 2.1 OASIS Standard (2021), with errata published in 2025
description: A JSON data model for cyber threat intelligence: indicators, observed data, threat actors, campaigns, malware, courses of action, and the relationships between them. | Relevant to regulated entities mainly through mandated reporting and sector information-sharing schemes, where the ISAC or supervisor expects machine-readable submissions rather than email.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: TAXII
fullName: Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information
description: The HTTPS application protocol for exchanging STIX content: collections to pull from, channels to subscribe to, and the API endpoints a sharing community agrees on. | Deploy it when you join a sharing community that runs one; there is no reason to adopt it in isolation.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 42001
description: A management system standard for artificial intelligence, built on the same Annex SL structure as ISO/IEC 27001: context, leadership, planning, support, operation, evaluation, improvement, with AI-specific controls covering impact assessment, data for AI systems, and lifecycle documentation. | It does not make you AI Act compliant on its own; the Act's harmonised standards are being written by CEN-CENELEC. But it is the management system regulators, customers and insurers can already audit against, and its documentation obligations line up closely with the Act's technical documentation requirements.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 23894
description: Guidance on managing risk specific to AI systems, applying the ISO 31000 risk management process to AI-specific sources of risk: data quality, model behaviour, autonomy, transparency, and human oversight. | Non-certifiable and deliberately procedural. Read it as the implementation companion when 42001 asks for an AI risk assessment and you need to decide what that actually contains.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: NIST AI RMF
statusStatement: AI RMF 1.0 (2023) plus the Generative AI Profile (2024)
description: A voluntary framework organised into four functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) for identifying and managing risks across the AI lifecycle, with a companion playbook of concrete actions. | The Generative AI Profile extends it to foundation-model risks: confabulation, data leakage, provenance, and the supply chain of models you did not train yourself.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: JTC 21
fullName: CEN-CENELEC JTC 21: Harmonised European Standards for AI
statusStatement: Standardisation request under the AI Act; deliverables in progress, none yet cited in the Official Journal
description: The joint technical committee drafting the harmonised European standards for the EU AI Act, covering risk management, data governance and data quality, transparency, human oversight, accuracy and robustness, and conformity assessment for high-risk AI systems. | Once cited in the Official Journal, conformity with these standards gives a presumption of conformity with the corresponding AI Act requirements, which is why anyone building high-risk AI in Europe should be tracking the drafts rather than waiting.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 5259
fullName: Data Quality for Analytics and Machine Learning
statusStatement: Multi-part series; core parts published from 2024
description: A series covering data quality for analytics and machine learning: vocabulary, quality measures, management requirements, a process framework, and governance of the data used to train and evaluate models. | It is the standards work that most directly addresses what "relevant, representative, free of errors and complete" is supposed to mean when a regulator says it about training data.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: OWASP LLM Top 10
statusStatement: 2025 edition (March 2025); part of the OWASP GenAI Security Project
description: The consensus risk list for applications built on large language models: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data and model poisoning, improper output handling, excessive agency, and more. | Directly relevant wherever an LLM touches governed data: a retrieval pipeline over regulated data inherits every one of these risks, and this is the list auditors have started asking about by name.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: OWASP API Top 10
description: The API-specific risk list: broken object level authorisation, broken authentication, broken object property level authorisation, unrestricted resource consumption, and the rest of the failures that dominate real API breaches. | Authorisation failures top the list because APIs expose object identifiers directly, the same shape of mistake that turns a data product output port into an unintended bulk export.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: OWASP ASVS
description: A catalogue of application security requirements organised into verification levels, written so each requirement can be tested rather than asserted. | Unlike the Top 10 lists, ASVS is a requirements standard: it is what you put in a supplier contract or a definition of done when "secure" has to survive contact with an auditor.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: OWASP SAMM
description: A maturity model for secure software delivery across five business functions (governance, design, implementation, verification, operations), each with streams scored at three maturity levels. | Its purpose is direction rather than certification: measure where you are, choose the next increment, re-measure. The output is a roadmap, which is what most secure-development clauses in regulation actually expect you to have.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: OWASP ML Top 10
statusStatement: Draft; superseded in practice by the GenAI project for LLM work
description: A risk list for classical machine learning systems: input manipulation, data poisoning, model inversion, membership inference, model theft, and transfer learning attacks. | Still the better reference for a trained-in-house model that is not a language model. Treat it as a checklist rather than a standard: the document has been in draft for years.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: CSA CCM
statusStatement: CCM v4.1: 197 control objectives in 17 domains; CAIQ and the STAR registry
description: A cloud-specific control framework of nearly two hundred control objectives across seventeen domains, with a shared responsibility model that says which controls belong to the provider and which to the customer. | The companion CAIQ questionnaire and the public STAR registry are what make it operationally useful: for most major cloud services, the answers already exist and can be diffed rather than requested.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISO/IEC 27017
description: A code of practice adding cloud-specific implementation guidance to the ISO/IEC 27002 controls, plus seven controls that exist only in a cloud context: shared roles, virtual machine hardening, administrator operations, monitoring, and segregation in virtual environments. | Certification is normally an extension of a 27001 audit rather than a standalone exercise.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: BSI C5
statusStatement: C5:2020: 121 criteria in 17 areas; attested under ISAE 3000
description: A criteria catalogue for cloud service security, assessed by an auditor and reported as an attestation rather than a certificate, so the customer receives a full report, including the auditor's findings, not just a pass mark. | The transparency criteria are the distinctive part: providers must disclose jurisdiction, data location, and the legal environment they operate under, which is exactly what a European data sovereignty review needs to see.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: EU Cloud CoC
statusStatement: Approved under GDPR Article 40 (2021); monitored by SCOPE Europe
description: A code of conduct for cloud providers acting as processors, formally approved by the Belgian data protection authority under GDPR Article 40 with an accredited monitoring body. | Adherence is one of the mechanisms GDPR explicitly recognises for demonstrating sufficient guarantees from a processor, which makes it a lighter alternative to bespoke due diligence when it is available.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: SOC 2
statusStatement: Trust Services Criteria (2017, revised points of focus 2022)
description: An attestation report by an independent auditor against five trust services criteria: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. A Type I report covers design at a point in time; Type II covers operating effectiveness over a period. | Not a certification and not a European instrument, but for SaaS vendors it is the de-facto entry ticket, and the Type II report is the evidence pack most third-party risk teams open first.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ISAE 3402
fullName: Assurance Reports on Controls at a Service Organization
statusStatement: Effective since 2011; the international counterpart to SSAE 18
description: The international assurance standard for reporting on controls at a service organisation that are relevant to its customers' financial reporting: the report an outsourced provider gives its clients' auditors. | Where SOC 2 answers security questions, ISAE 3402 answers the auditor's question about whether your controls can be relied on in someone else's financial statements. ISAE 3000 covers the same mechanics for non-financial subject matter, including BSI C5.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: SPDX
statusStatement: SPDX 3.0 (2024), 3.1 in review; version 2.2.1 published as ISO/IEC 5962:2021
description: A bill-of-materials standard for describing software components, licences, copyrights and security references. SPDX 3.0 generalised the model to cover builds, AI models, datasets and services alongside packages. | The dataset and AI profiles matter here: they are the closest thing to a standard way of shipping a machine-readable declaration of what data a model was trained on.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: CycloneDX
statusStatement: CycloneDX v1.7, published as ECMA-424 (2nd edition, 2025); SBOM, SaaSBOM, ML-BOM, CBOM and VEX
description: A bill-of-materials standard designed for security use cases, covering software, services, hardware, machine learning models and cryptographic assets, with VEX support for stating whether a vulnerability actually affects you. | The ML-BOM and CBOM profiles are directly regulatory: one documents model and dataset provenance, the other inventories cryptography ahead of post-quantum migration mandates.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: SLSA
statusStatement: v1.2 current, adding a source track; v1.0 released 2023
description: A framework of graduated levels for build integrity and provenance: what a build platform must guarantee at each of build levels L0 to L3, and what the resulting provenance attestation must say about how an artefact was produced. Version 1.2 adds a source track alongside it. | It is the concrete answer to "prove this binary came from that source", the requirement underneath most modern software supply chain expectations.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: Sigstore
description: Signing infrastructure for software artefacts using short-lived certificates tied to an OIDC identity, with signatures recorded in a public transparency log. | The keyless model is why it gets adopted: no long-lived signing key to protect, and the transparency log gives an auditor something to check independently.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: in-toto
statusStatement: CNCF graduated project (2025); in-toto Attestation Framework v1.0
description: A framework for cryptographically verifying that every step of a software supply chain was carried out by the intended party, in the intended order, on the intended materials. | Its attestation format is the substrate SLSA provenance is carried in, so adopt it as plumbing rather than as a programme of its own.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: Gaia-X
statusStatement: Trust Framework with compliance and clearing house services
description: A trust framework for European data infrastructure: self-descriptions of participants, services and resources as verifiable credentials, validated against machine-readable compliance rules by clearing houses. | The idea worth borrowing regardless of your view on the initiative is that jurisdiction, data location and applicable law become attributes of a service that a machine can check, not claims in a sales deck.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: Dataspace Protocol
statusStatement: Release 2025-1; maintained by the Eclipse Dataspace Working Group
description: A protocol for sovereign data exchange: catalogue discovery, contract negotiation over ODRL usage policies, and a transfer process that hands off to whatever data plane the parties agree on. | It is the machinery that makes "data stays under the provider's terms" enforceable across organisational boundaries, and the reference protocol for EU data space implementations such as the Eclipse Dataspace Components.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: DSSC Blueprint
statusStatement: Blueprint 3.0, the concluding version of the DSSC project
description: The European Commission-funded reference blueprint for data spaces: the building blocks a data space needs for identity, trust, contracts, vocabularies, and data exchange, with the standards that fill each slot. | Read it as the index to the sector data spaces being built under the Data Governance Act and the Data Act: it tells you which specification each participating initiative expects you to implement.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: IDS-RAM
fullName: International Data Spaces Reference Architecture Model
statusStatement: RAM 4 is the stable edition, with 2026-1 in draft; the connector concept lives on in the Dataspace Protocol
description: The architecture model that introduced the data space vocabulary in Europe: connectors, identity providers, clearing houses, vocabulary hubs, and the sovereign exchange of data between them. | Its concepts survive; its own protocol layer has effectively been superseded by the Dataspace Protocol, which is where the interoperability work has moved.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: SAML
description: The XML standard for exchanging authentication and authorisation assertions between an identity provider and a service provider. It is what most enterprise single sign-on still runs on. | It matters here because access control evidence starts with authentication: an auditor asking who could reach a data set is really asking which identity provider vouched for them, and what the assertion claimed.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: OAuth 2.0
statusStatement: RFC 6749 with a large family of extensions
description: The delegated authorisation framework behind almost every modern API: a client obtains a scoped, time limited token instead of the user's credentials. | Scopes and token lifetimes are the enforcement points a control framework leans on, and token issuance logs are the evidence that least privilege was more than an intention.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: OpenID Connect
description: An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: the ID token carries verified claims about who the user is, alongside the access token that says what they may do. | Its certification programme is the practical part. Where a control requires federated identity, pointing at a certified implementation is a shorter conversation than describing your own.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: SCIM
description: A schema and REST protocol for provisioning and deprovisioning user accounts and groups between systems. | Deprovisioning is the audit finding it prevents. Joiner, mover and leaver controls only hold if account removal propagates automatically to every tool holding data, which is precisely what SCIM automates.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: DID
description: Globally unique identifiers that resolve to a document describing how to authenticate the subject, without depending on a central registry. | The reason it appears on a compliance map: European data spaces and agent ecosystems both need a party to prove who it is across organisational boundaries, and a DID is the identifier those trust frameworks are built on.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: Verifiable Credentials
description: A data model for tamper evident claims that a holder can present and a verifier can check cryptographically, without contacting the issuer. | Gaia-X self descriptions and the EU digital identity wallet both rest on it. It is how an assertion such as "this service is certified and hosted in the EU" becomes machine checkable rather than a claim in a brochure.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: ACP
statusStatement: Merged into A2A under the Linux Foundation (2025)
description: An open protocol for agents to discover each other and exchange tasks, launched by IBM Research in 2025 for the BeeAI platform and donated to the Linux Foundation with it. | Listed for completeness rather than as a target: the effort has been folding into A2A, so new work should look there first.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: AG-UI
description: An event based protocol between agent backends and user facing applications, covering streaming output, tool calls, state updates and human approval steps. | Its compliance relevance is human oversight. Where the AI Act expects a person to be able to intervene, the interaction protocol is where that intervention is actually implemented and logged.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

name: AP2
governanceStatement: Google; standardisation moving to the FIDO Alliance
description: A protocol for payments initiated by agents, using signed mandates and verifiable credentials so that intent, authorisation and execution can each be proven after the fact. | Payments are where agent autonomy meets regulated ground: strong customer authentication, audit trails and liability all need an answer before an agent may spend anything. The FIDO Alliance has taken up the standardisation work through its agentic authentication and payments working groups.
:LABEL: LandscapeEntry;DataRegulationLandscapeEntry

description: Secure read access is a direct technical means for restricting who may access personal data and for supporting confidentiality controls; applicability and the appropriate measures remain context- and risk-dependent.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping

name: Secure read access to HIPAA context
description: Secure read access is a direct technical means for the HIPAA Security Rule access-control standard that allows access to ePHI only by authorised persons.

:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping

name: Secure read access to NIST SP 800-53 context
description: Secure read access is a direct technical means for enforcing approved authorisations for logical access to information and system resources; selecting and configuring the policy remains an organisational control decision.

regulatoryRequirementReference: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 — Access Enforcement

name: Secure write access to GDPR context
description: Secure write access is a direct technical means for protecting personal data against unauthorised alteration and for supporting integrity controls; it is only one part of the required technical and organisational measures.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping

name: Secure write access to HIPAA context
description: Secure write access is a direct technical means for protecting ePHI from improper alteration or destruction under the HIPAA Security Rule integrity standard.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping

name: Secure write access to NIST SP 800-53 context
description: Secure write access is a direct technical means for detecting and protecting against unauthorised changes to information; integrity monitoring and write controls still require policy selection and operational evidence.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping
regulatoryRequirementReference: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-7 — Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity

name: Validation and contract binding to NIST SP 800-53 context
description: Validation and contract binding are a direct technical means for checking information inputs and handling invalid inputs predictably; a contract implementation must still select and enforce the applicable constraints.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping
regulatoryRequirementReference: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-10 — Information Input Validation

name: Validation and contract binding to BCBS 239 context
description: Validation and contract binding are a direct technical means for checking accuracy and integrity constraints on risk and reporting data; BCBS 239 still expects broader governance, aggregation and reporting controls beyond pipeline validation.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping

name: Metadata registration to GDPR context
description: Metadata registration is a direct technical means for capturing purposes, data categories, recipients, transfers, retention and security measures needed for records of processing; a catalogue record is not automatically a complete Article 30 record.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping
regulatoryRequirementReference: GDPR Article 30 — Records of processing activities

name: Metadata registration to ISO/IEC 11179 context
description: Metadata registration directly aligns with the ISO/IEC 11179 metadata-registry family, including registration of dataset metadata, provenance, quality, fitness and risk information.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping
regulatoryRequirementReference: ISO/IEC 11179-33:2023 — Metamodel for data set registration

name: Metadata registration to BCBS 239 context
description: Metadata registration is a direct technical means for documenting ownership, lineage, definitions and quality characteristics required by a coherent risk-data architecture; BCBS 239 does not prescribe a specific registry product.
:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping
regulatoryRequirementReference: BCBS 239 Principle 2 — Data architecture and IT infrastructure

name: Failure isolation to NIST SP 800-53 context

:LABEL: ComponentRegulatoryMapping
regulatoryRequirementReference: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-13 — Predictable Failure Prevention
